lesson.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

sources.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts

steps.title: Create the conflicting example repo
steps.instructions: In an empty folder run `git init -b main`, commit app.txt with `title=App` and `footer=v1`, then on `git checkout -b feature/login` make three commits (title=Login, add login.txt, footer=login). Switch to main, commit title=Home then footer=v2, run `git checkout feature/login`, and run `git branch -a` to confirm there is no remotes/origin copy.

targets.caption: Confirm the feature branch has no remote copy (no remotes/origin/... line)
app.txt with the title= and footer= lines that both branches change

explanations.topic: Use git branch -a to check whether the feature branch was already pushed, and so whether it is safe to rebase
Two choices on a conflict during rebase: abort the rebase or resolve the conflict
Rebase sets your commits aside and reapplies them one by one, so each commit can cause its own conflict
The example repo: three feature commits and two main commits; two of the feature commits will conflict

hints: Make every commit with git add and git commit before you switch branches. Otherwise the changes go with you to the other branch.
On feature/login, change line 1 and line 2 in separate commits, and add login.txt in its own commit, so you have three commits.
On main, change the same two lines to different values (title=Home, then footer=v2). This is what makes the conflicts happen later.
Run git log --oneline --all --graph to check that main has 2 new commits and feature/login has 3, both starting from the initial commit.
common_mistakes: Creating feature/login after making the main commits. The branch then includes them and there is nothing to rebase.
Leaving changes uncommitted before git checkout, so they move to the other branch.
Putting several edits into one commit instead of three separate feature commits.
Forgetting to switch back to feature/login before the rebase step.
Running git branch -a and seeing a remotes/... copy of the feature branch, but planning to rebase anyway.
steps.code:
git init -b main
printf 'title=App\nfooter=v1\n' > app.txt
git add app.txt && git commit -m "Initial app"
git checkout -b feature/login
# line 1 -> title=Login, commit
# add login.txt, commit
# line 2 -> footer=login, commit
git checkout main
# line 1 -> title=Home, commit
# line 2 -> footer=v2, commit
git checkout feature/login
git branch -a

steps.title: Start the rebase onto main
steps.instructions: On your feature branch run `git rebase main`; it stops with a CONFLICT in app.txt. Run `git status` to see the rebase in progress and the remaining commits.

targets.caption: Rebase pauses on the first conflicting commit
git status confirms the rebase is paused
Commits still waiting to be applied

explanations.topic: A conflict pauses the rebase instead of aborting it
git status shows which commit failed and how many remain
Fixing rebase conflicts works like fixing merge conflicts: Git inserts conflict markers

hints: Make sure you're on your feature branch (git branch), then rebase it onto main.
Run `git rebase main` from the feature branch. A CONFLICT message is the expected result.
After the conflict, run `git status`. It should say a rebase is in progress and list the next commands to do.
If you see 'Current branch is up to date', you're probably on main or the branches don't diverge. Check out feature/login first.
common_mistakes: Running `git rebase main` while on main instead of the feature branch.
Running `git rebase --abort` on seeing the CONFLICT, which undoes the rebase you need for the next step.
Using `git merge main` instead of `git rebase main`, which creates a merge commit instead of replaying commits.
Not committing everything in step 1, so the rebase refuses to start because of unstaged changes.

steps.title: Resolve the first conflict
steps.instructions: Open app.txt, delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers keeping the line that should stay (e.g. title=Login), then `git add app.txt` and run `git status`.

targets.caption: Remove the conflict markers and keep the line that should stay

explanations.topic: Remove the markers and pick the code that should stay
Run git add for every conflicted file once it is fixed
Rebase uses git rebase --continue instead of git commit

hints: Open the conflicted file (app.txt) in your editor and look for the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines.
Keep only the version of the line that should remain, then delete all three marker lines.
Save the file, run `git add app.txt`, then run `git status` to confirm it says all conflicts are fixed.
common_mistakes: Leaving one of the marker lines (often =======) in the file.
Forgetting to save the file before running git add.
Running `git commit` instead of staging and moving on to `git rebase --continue`.
Keeping both versions of the line when only one should stay.

steps.title: Continue the rebase
steps.instructions: Run `git rebase --continue`; when vim opens for the commit message, press Escape and type `:wq` to keep it. Git applies the non-conflicting commit automatically and pauses again on the next conflict.

targets.caption: Continue the rebase instead of committing
Git pauses again on the next commit

explanations.topic: Leaving vim with Escape then :wq keeps the commit message
Last commit conflicts again, git pauses

hints: During a rebase you don't commit. After staging your fixes, ask git to move on to the next commit.
Run `git rebase --continue`. If git says files are still unmerged, run `git add <file>` first.
When vim opens with the commit message, press Escape and type `:wq` then Enter to save and close it.
Git should then apply the next commit and stop at a new CONFLICT for the third commit. That conflict is expected.
common_mistakes: Running `git commit` instead of `git rebase --continue`.
Running continue before `git add`-ing the resolved file, which makes git refuse to continue.
Getting stuck in vim: typing :wq without pressing Escape first, or using :q! and aborting the message.
Thinking the new CONFLICT means something broke. The third commit is meant to conflict.
Running `git rebase --abort` by mistake, which throws away the rebase progress.

steps.title: Resolve the last conflict and finish
steps.instructions: Remove the conflict markers in app.txt keeping the lines you want, then run `git add app.txt` and `git rebase --continue`, saving with `:wq`. Run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph` to confirm the rebase finished.

targets.caption: Resolve the last conflict in app.txt
git status confirms rebase is over

explanations.topic: No commits left concludes the rebase
Use git status to confirm you're not rebasing

hints: Resolve this conflict the same way as the first one: edit app.txt, then stage it and continue.
Delete every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> line and keep the content you want, e.g. footer=login.
Run `git add app.txt` then `git rebase --continue`; save the commit message in the editor with :wq.
Run `git status`: it should say 'On branch ...' with no rebase in progress, and `git log --oneline --graph` should show your commits on top of main.
common_mistakes: Leaving conflict markers in app.txt before running git add.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue.
Forgetting to git add app.txt, so git rebase --continue complains about unmerged paths.
Getting stuck in the vim editor instead of saving with :wq.
Running git rebase --skip and dropping the commit's changes.
